transcript: Alright, it's finally time. Let's talk spoilers for immersive Phantom. I will be spoiling some very key moments of this experience, so you have been warned. Let's start with the beginning because the opening scene of the show is one of the most magical things I have ever experienced. Adam Giery is teaching you the masquerade dance. And then the back wall opens, the room fills with light, and you are transported into this opulent ball. There's a giant ensemble of actors dressed in ornate, colorful costumes and it is truly jaw dropping. Like words cannot describe just how magical it was. And then it's the one two punch of that scene, immediately followed by the chandelier rising and being transported back in time. After that you're like, okay, this is gonna be something special. Let's also talk about the new material added to this version of the show as they brought in some of the Phantom's backstory from the movie and even expanded on it. There is an entire sequence in the show about the carnival that he grew up in and is eventually rescued from by Madame Giry. They also bring in learn to Be Lonely from the film, which, fine, it's definitely the worst song in the show, but I do like it more here than I did in the film, so that's a win. And it is nice to hear Jerry have a song because otherwise she doesn't really sing in this. I also thought it Was really clever how they would sometimes break you down into smaller subgroups for some of the more intimate scenes. There's the trio of basement scenes and then the trio of dressing room scenes, where everyone is seeing the same three scenes, but depending on which group you're in will determine which order you watch them. And the dressing room scenes in particular are so seamless. Like, they flow so nicely into one another that you really wouldn't know what's happening unless you knew to look for it. And that's true of, like, every part of this experience. It's also perfectly timed. You never run into any of the other groups. You never hear sound bleed from other rooms. And mad props to Diane Paulus and team for figuring all of this out logistically, because I truly don't know how they did it. Finally, let's talk about the ending. Cause I thought it was a really smart twist on the ending of the musical. You get, I think, one of the best allusions in the show, where Christine vanishes in the cloak. But then they choose to end it with a much simpler moment, where everyone takes off their mask, and we are looking directly at the Phantom, and he sees us, and we see him. And it's just this moment of human connection. This experience really humanizes the Phantom more so than past iterations of this material have. Because, yes, this production delivers on the spectacle in spades. But, It also takes full advantage of the intimacy of seeing the show in these smaller groups and experiencing these performances from feet away. And I think that's what takes it from a really cool experience that you do once and then you're done, to a really great experience that you wanna experience multiple times. You wanna see multiple actors take on these roles. Because the show, at its core, is not about the spectacle. It's about the characters.
